narrative:
The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 21.3, it sits far below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, signaling that the model saw this as a major risk for bar exam performance.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor, but it worked in your favor. At 3.20 it is only slightly below the accepted students’ average of 3.23, giving the model a modest reason to believe you could still succeed.

Third in importance was your class ranking in the third year of law school. Ranking in the second decile is noticeably weaker than the average fifth-to-sixth decile among accepted students, and this gap pulled the prediction back toward failure.

Taken together, the low LSAT and weaker third-year ranking outweighed the small positive signal from your GPA, leading to the 65% failure risk that caused the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on improving your bar exam readiness. Consider retaking the LSAT for a stronger score, seek targeted bar-prep tutoring, and look for law schools or programs that offer additional academic support. These steps can directly address the areas the model flagged as highest risk. (248 words)
